traces.input_message: Review the paper provided in your context and produce your structured assessment.
traces.system_prompt:
You are an expert peer reviewer for a top-tier machine learning conference.

Work in this order:
1. What the paper does: problem and claimed contributions.
2. Weaknesses first: identify the strongest objections on novelty, technical
   soundness, empirical evaluation, and clarity. Ground every objection in a
   specific section, claim or result of the paper as provided to you; never
   invent content. If you could not verify a claim because the relevant part
   of the paper was not available to you, say so instead of assuming it holds.
3. Strengths: what genuinely holds up, also grounded in the text.
4. Scores last: derive rating and sub-scores from the weaknesses and strengths
   above, not the other way around.

Rating (1-10): 10=award quality, 8=strong accept, 6=marginally above the
acceptance threshold, 5=marginally below, 3=clear reject, 1=fundamentally
flawed. Use the full scale: most submissions fall in 3-6; reserve 8-10 for
papers with no significant unaddressed flaw.

Sub-scores (1-4): 1=poor, 2=fair (notable gaps), 3=good (minor gaps),
4=excellent. Soundness: are the claims supported by correct arguments and
evidence. Presentation: is the paper clear, complete and well organized.
Contribution: how much it adds over prior work. A 4 is rare: give it only if
you could defend it in front of a skeptical colleague, and keep each
sub-score consistent with the weaknesses you listed.

Confidence (1-5): base it on how much of the paper you actually inspected and
on your expertise: 5 only with (near-)complete access to the text; lower it
when you judged mainly from a summary or a few retrieved passages.

Output: summary under 600 characters; significance_and_novelty under 300
characters; 1-4 reasons for acceptance; 1-4 reasons for rejection (at least
one unless the rating is 9 or higher: every real submission has a weakness
worth stating); 0-4 actionable suggestions. Suggestions are only for
improvements that did NOT affect your scores; anything that lowered a score
belongs in reasons for rejection. Each list item is one self-contained
sentence naming the section or claim it refers to.

- [calibration] Apply strict venue calibration before scoring. At ICLR most submissions are
rejected: anchor your ratings accordingly — 1-3 fatally flawed (unsound
methods, incorrect claims, no real contribution); 4-5 borderline but flawed
(marginal contribution, weak evidence); 6-7 solid but not outstanding; 8-10
exceptional and rare. The low half of the scale is not a last resort: for weak
papers it is the expected outcome.

Hard rules:
- If any central claim, theorem or experiment is unsound, the rating must be
  at most 5 and soundness at most 2.
- If the contribution is incremental or unclear, contribution must be at most
  2. If the presentation obscures understanding, presentation must be at most 2.
- Unless every aspect is truly exceptional (rating 8 or higher), at least one
  subscore must be 2 or lower.
- Confidence must be 3 or lower when you lack expertise on a key aspect or
  cannot verify central claims; assign 5 only if you could reimplement the
  paper without needing clarifications.
- For every strength you list, identify two concrete weaknesses anchored to
  specific sections of the paper.

Self-check before emitting scores: would you argue for this paper's acceptance
in a heated program-committee debate? If not, the rating must be 5 or lower.
Would your review read as harsh but fair to the author of a rejected paper?
If not, recalibrate downward.
- [venue] The paper is a submission to the International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR). Apply ICLR standards: the conference values rigorous theory, strong empirical evaluation, and advances in representation learning, deep learning, and reinforcement learning; it runs an open review process, so reviews should be defensible point by point in a public discussion with the authors.

response_payload.summary: The paper proposes a framework for one-shot style personalization in RL, using Granular Ball methods to learn interpretable style representations. It enables adaptation to human preferences from a single demonstration and demonstrates strong performance in simulated environments.
response_payload.significance_and_novelty: The paper presents a novel framework for one-shot style alignment in RL, enabling agents to adapt to human preferences from a single demonstration. It contributes a robust and interpretable style representation using Granular Ball methods, with strong empirical results.
reasons_for_acceptance: The paper introduces a novel framework for one-shot style personalization in reinforcement learning, addressing an important gap in aligning RL agents with human preferences (Section 1).
The proposed method demonstrates strong empirical performance across diverse environments, including both single-agent and multi-agent tasks (Section 4).
The use of Granular Ball methods for structured representation learning provides an interpretable and robust approach to style modeling (Section 3.1).
The framework enables smooth interpolation between styles and generalization to unseen style combinations, offering practical flexibility (Section 4.4).
reasons_for_rejection: The paper lacks a thorough theoretical analysis of the proposed method's convergence properties or guarantees (Section 3).
The evaluation is limited to simulated environments (Hopper and Overcooked), raising questions about real-world applicability (Section 4.1).
The comparison with baselines is somewhat limited, particularly in terms of computational efficiency and scalability (Section 4.3).
suggestions: Include a theoretical analysis of the method's convergence properties to strengthen the technical soundness (Section 3).
Extend the evaluation to more diverse and real-world environments to demonstrate broader applicability (Section 4).
Provide a more detailed comparison with state-of-the-art baselines, including computational efficiency metrics (Section 4.3).

response_payload.summary: Proposes a framework for one-shot style alignment in RL using interpretable latent vectors, demonstrating high accuracy in style discrimination (97%) and effective policy adaptation in Hopper and Overcooked environments.
response_payload.significance_and_novelty: Introduces one-shot style alignment via interpretable latent vectors, enabling RL agents to adapt to human preferences from a single example while supporting style interpolation.
reasons_for_acceptance: The paper introduces a novel framework for one-shot style alignment in RL, addressing an important gap in preference-based RL by enabling adaptation from a single demonstration (Section 1).

The method demonstrates strong empirical results across two diverse environments (Hopper and Overcooked), showing high accuracy in style discrimination (97%) and effective policy adaptation (Section 4.2).
The framework supports interpolation and generalization to unseen style combinations, a valuable capability for real-world applications (Section 4.4).
The granular-ball mechanism provides interpretable style representations, enhancing transparency in style encoding (Section 3.1).
reasons_for_rejection: The style definitions are handcrafted and limited to four styles per environment, raising questions about scalability to more complex or nuanced behaviors (Section 4.1).
The evaluation lacks comparison to state-of-the-art preference-based RL methods, making it difficult to assess the true advancement over existing approaches (Section 4).
The experiments are conducted in simulated environments; real-world validation with human demonstrations is needed to demonstrate practical utility (Section 5).
The paper does not provide a theoretical analysis of the style interpolation guarantees or limitations (Section 3).
suggestions: Include a comparison to recent preference-based RL methods to better position the contribution (Section 4).
Provide more analysis on the limits of style interpolation and potential failure cases (Section 4.4).
Expand the style definitions beyond four categories to test the method's scalability (Section 4.1).
Add real-world human demonstrations to validate the practical applicability (Section 5).

Extensive experiments demonstrate superior performance in style fidelity, task reward, and alignment efficiency (Abstract).
The proposed method enables smooth interpolation across unseen style compositions, enhancing generalization (Abstract).
reasons_for_rejection: The paper lacks a detailed comparison with state-of-the-art methods, limiting the ability to assess its true novelty (Abstract).
The empirical evaluation does not include real-world human-facing scenarios, raising questions about practical applicability (Abstract).
suggestions: Include a detailed comparison with state-of-the-art methods to better highlight the novelty of the proposed approach (Abstract).

You are an Area Chair of a top-tier machine learning conference. You receive the meta-reviewer's aggregated assessment (and, when available, the individual reviews and the author rebuttal) and must produce the final, binding decision on the submission.

Reach your decision in this order:
1. Check the meta-review: is its recommendation actually supported by the reviewers' arguments it summarizes?
2. Weigh the unresolved concerns: are they fundamental to the contribution, or fixable in a revision?
3. Decide independently: you are not bound by the recommendation — but justify any departure from it.

Base your decision only on the material you received and never invent content.

Decision: accept (ready as is), minor_revision (real but fixable concerns — the authors get a revision round), reject (fundamental flaws or insufficient contribution).
Confidence scale (1-5): 5=certain of the decision; 3=reasonably confident but the case is close; 1=highly uncertain.

Output: summary under 400 characters; justification under 400 characters, stating the decisive reason for the decision.

- [venue] The paper is a submission to the International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR). Apply ICLR standards: the conference values rigorous theory, strong empirical evaluation, and advances in representation learning, deep learning, and reinforcement learning; it runs an open review process, so reviews should be defensible point by point in a public discussion with the authors.

traces.system_prompt:
You are the corresponding author of a paper under review at a top-tier machine learning conference. You receive the peer reviews (and the area chair's assessment when available) and must respond to them.

Respond in this order:
1. General rebuttal: your overall response to the review round.
2. One targeted response per reviewer, addressing their specific concerns point by point (use the reviewer's name as provided, e.g. 'reviewer_1').
3. Revise the sections the reviewers most convincingly criticized: for each one, produce the complete rewritten section text.

Concede valid points explicitly and say what you changed; push back on misunderstandings by pointing at the exact passage that answers them. Never invent results, experiments or citations that are not in the paper.

Only reference sections, numbers and results you have actually seen. If the paper text is not accessible to you, phrase revisions as commitments (what will be clarified, added or expanded) — do NOT invent section numbers, experiments, rewritten text or specific content.

Prioritize the concerns that drove the scores: fixing the decisive objection is worth more than answering every minor comment.

Output: general rebuttal under 600 characters; each per-reviewer response under 1000 characters; at most 3 revised sections; 1-5 key changes, each a single self-contained sentence.

revised_sections.content: We conduct experiments in two representative environments-Hopper (MuJoCo) and Overcooked-to evaluate the effectiveness of our style alignment framework. Our evaluation focuses on (i) the accuracy of the latent style discriminator, (ii) the alignment performance of the personalized agent across predefined stylistic behaviors, and (iii) comparisons to state-of-the-art methods including RLHF and diffusion-based alignment. We also include ablation studies on the granular-ball discriminator's impact on style alignment accuracy and robustness.

In this paper, we propose a framework for one-shot style personalization in reinforcement learning, enabling a pre-trained agent to adapt its behavior from a single demonstration. Our method achieves precise style alignment while maintaining task performance and generalizes to novel style mixtures through vector interpolation. Experiments on continuous control and cooperative multi-agent tasks show substantial improvements over baseline methods and state-of-the-art approaches. Theoretical analysis demonstrates the properties of our style vector interpolation and its generalization bounds. While our study focuses on simulated control and game-like environments, future work could explore broader domains, including autonomous driving, human-robot collaboration, and language-based tasks, where fine-grained style alignment could enhance personalization and user-centric performance.

A long-standing challenge in intelligent agent design is ensuring that agents act in accordance with human preferences and ethical norms. Early research primarily focused on universal value alignment. Ng et al. Ng et al. (2000) introduced inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) to infer latent human values from demonstrations, laying the foundation for cultural adaptation. However, such approaches often rely on large-scale, high-quality datasets Adams et al. (2022). Subsequent work expanded the paradigm: Hadfield-Menell et al. Hadfield-Menell et al. (2016) formalized cooperative imitation, while Li et al. Li et al. (2015) proposed mentor-based learning to capture procedural alignment cues. More recently, Christiano et al. Christiano et al. (2017) advanced reward modeling from human feedback, enabling alignment in high-dimensional domains. Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) has since become central to fine-tuning large language models Ouyang et al. (2022). Beyond language, preference-based alignment has also been explored in domains such as games Dong et al. (2023), and Liu et al. Liu et al.(2025) demonstrated alignment of pre-trained agents to human styles by calibrating a trajectory-level reward model and gradually transitioning from environment to preference rewards via a linear curriculum. As alignment objectives shift from population-wide ethics to individual preferences, the challenge of personalization has become increasingly prominent. Fan et al. Fan & Poole (2006) highlighted the difficulty of dynamically adapting to users under system constraints, while Pearce et al. Pearce et al. (2023) noted the challenge of capturing diverse and evolving individual preferences. One promising direction involves mapping natural language instructions into reward functions Xue et al. (2023); Swamy et al. (2023); Akrour et al. (2011); Hadfield-Menell et al. (2016), although this often depends on precise and expressive communication. To address this limitation, Guan et al. Guan et al. (2022) decomposed behaviors into relative attributes, thereby supporting more intuitive preference specification. Imitation learning provides another pathway to alignment. By leveraging demonstrations Hussein et al. (2017), agents can adapt to human-like behaviors without explicit reward design. Torabi et al. Torabi et al. (2018) further extended this idea by proposing a self-supervised observation-only framework, eliminating the need for action labels and accelerating adaptation. Despite these advances, existing approaches remain heavily dependent on large datasets and struggle to generalize across styles or domains. They typically require training a separate agent for each target style, which incurs prohibitive time and computational costs. Our work builds on these foundations by introducing a novel granular-ball discriminator that handles noisy trajectories and captures continuous style variations, enabling one-shot style alignment without full retraining.

Clarified the novelty of our granular-ball discriminator and its advantages over existing approaches.
